title:
Comment of Trevor Love in Docket(s)/Project(s) P-15423-000
Submission Date: 10/20/2026

documents.name: 151774.txt
documents.text:
Trevor Love, Lakewood, WA.
Re: DeepGreen Cook Inlet SPV, LLC — Preliminary Permit Application, Project No. P-15423-000

I am writing as a private citizen in support of underwater data-center research, with conditions. I filed comments in the same spirit on this applicant's Western Passage application (Project No. P-15424-000), and the same reasoning applies here — strengthened, because this project is larger and the waterway is less forgiving.

Large land-based data centers keep being sited in communities where their water use and power demand raise costs and strain infrastructure. Moving compute underwater, powered by tidal energy, is one of the few alternatives that actually sidesteps those problems instead of pushing them onto residents. I want to see this concept tested seriously — not blocked by default.

But the scale proposed here is not a pilot: roughly 330 to 350 tidal turbines and 66 subsea-compute hives, about 100 megawatts, in the East Foreland corridor of Upper Cook Inlet — a bottleneck that endangered Cook Inlet beluga whales and migrating salmon move through. "Novel concept, novel problems" applies with more force, not less:

1.  Make acoustic impact a permit condition. Belugas navigate and hunt by sound, and NOAA's recovery plan for this population names in-water noise a high-concern threat. The permit's study phase should require publicly reported, independently measured acoustic-impact studies — noise budgets with actual decibel figures — before any license application moves forward. The same study plan should cover thermal discharge from the hives' passive cooling and effects on salmon migration through the corridor. Sound dampening is an engineering problem with engineering answers; require the answers on paper first.

2.  Phase it small. Where the Western Passage application described a phased first step, this one describes the full array. FERC should expect measured acoustic and ecological data from a small initial deployment — a limited number of turbines and hives — before any larger buildout is licensed. Small-scale proof is what makes the public willing to cooperate with the bigger version later.

3.  Require a public slack-tide power plan. Tidal generation falls toward zero at slack water, several times a day, every day. A data center drawing up to 100 megawatts does not pause with the tide — so the power comes from storage, from curtailing the compute load, or from the Alaska Railbelt Grid. One hundred megawatts is on the order of the Kenai Peninsula's entire peak demand. The study phase should require the applicant to state on the record where the power comes from at slack tide, and any grid draw should be measured, capped, and public — the project should not quietly become one of the region's largest grid loads while advertising that it supports the grid.

4.  Independent review of the studies. Environmental studies paid for by the applicant should be reviewed by evaluators with no financial tie to the company, so the public can trust the numbers — and claims the application makes about third-party infrastructure should be verified with the parties named.

Endangered species protections must be respected in this process — NOAA's best estimate for Cook Inlet belugas is about 331 animals — but wildlife concern alone should not be a veto on innovation. The standard should be: measure the impact, engineer the mitigation, verify it independently, and scale only when the numbers hold.

A preliminary permit authorizes studies, not construction. The studies it authorizes are exactly what will define whether this project deserves a license — so the conditions should be set now.

Trevor Love
